blocks.text: 在麻省理工学院（MIT），数学家们在周一一场题为“AI 与社会：数学的未来”的小组讨论中，探讨了上述问题以及其他疑问。来自 MIT、哈佛大学、西北大学和纽约大学的顶尖数学家——各自都是所在领域的专家——坐下来进行了一场对话，话题涉及 AI 数学的质量、AI 如何挑战由来已久的研究规范，以及数学家不断演变的机会，无论他们是拥抱机器，还是坚持做“AI 纯素食者”。

blocks.text: 这场内容广泛的讨论在 MIT 3 号楼一间座无虚席的阶梯教室举行，由科学作家、《代码中的证明》（The Proof in the Code）一书作者 Kevin Hartnett 主持，参与讨论的嘉宾包括：MIT 塞西尔与艾达·格林职业发展数学助理教授 Jacopo Borga；哈佛大学乔治·帕特南纯粹与应用数学教授 Michael Hopkins；西北大学萨拉·丽贝卡·罗兰数学教授 Bryna Kra；以及纽约大学柯朗数学科学研究所数学教授 Tristan Buckmaster。

blocks.text: “数学在过去两个月里的变化，比过去 100 年还要大，”Kra 说。她提醒道，AI 的力量将改变数学家的定义，也将改变以有意义的方式推进人类知识所需的条件。“这就像《双城记》开篇第一句：‘这是最好的时代，这是最坏的时代。’这是一个非常激动人心的时刻……同时也令人恐惧。”

blocks.text: AI 的冲刺

inlines.text: AI 的冲刺

blocks.text: 过去十年，人工智能取得了稳步进展，这在很大程度上要归功于数学家自己——他们出于好奇，一直在打磨 AI 模型，让它们去解决已有已知答案的问题。这些早期练习被证明是成功的，最引人注目的是在 2025 年。那年夏天，在国际数学奥林匹克竞赛上，谷歌 DeepMind 的 AI 模型迅速解出了向全球最优秀的高中数学选手提出的大部分题目，达到金牌水平。

blocks.text: 2026 年，AI 的能力实现了飞跃。在若干案例中，科学家发现模型能够解决开放式研究问题——即没有已知答案的数学问题。随后在 9 月，OpenAI 发布了一项震动整个领域的公告：该公司将数千个 AI 智能体集中到一个单一挑战上，88 小时后，这些智能体给出了一个与纳维-斯托克斯方程相关的证明——这是千禧年大奖难题之一，也是七个无法解决的数学圣杯问题之一。

blocks.text: It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep.

blocks.text: AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit?

blocks.text: At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.”

inlines.text: At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.”

blocks.text: The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences.

blocks.text: “Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.”

blocks.text: AI’s sprint

inlines.text: AI’s sprint

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.

inlines.text: Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.

blocks.text: Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.

inlines.text: Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.

blocks.text: In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails.

blocks.text: OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement.

blocks.text: OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research.

blocks.text: New norms

inlines.text: New norms

blocks.text: For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority.

inlines.text: For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority.

blocks.text: “It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.”

blocks.text: AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances.

blocks.text: “Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.”

For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas.
